title: Lifetime Deals for Agencies 2026: The License Tier Trap
desc: Lifetime deals for agencies in 2026: why the license tier and not the price decides the buy, what AppSumo's terms say about client work, and 5 checks to run first.
keywords: lifetime deals for agencies, best lifetime deals for agencies 2026, appsumo for agencies, can agencies use appsumo deals for clients, appsumo license tier, appsumo reselling policy, appsumo client work, lifetime software deals agency
cta: Want your agency stack and pipeline built properly?
body:
Short version: lifetime deals are a legitimate way for an agency to cut software costs, but the number that decides whether a deal is a good buy is not the price. It is the license tier. AppSumo's own support documentation confirms that once a deal sells out, the only option left in your account is to downgrade, because there are no higher tiers left to buy. An agency that buys Tier 1 to test, wins three clients, and comes back to upgrade can find the door closed. Buy for the client count you expect in twelve months, not the one you have this week.

That rule is worth more than any list of deals, because deals rotate weekly and the rule does not. Everything below was verified against AppSumo's Terms of Use and help centre on August 31, 2026, including a reselling clause that appears in three places with three different penalties.

The short answer for agency buyers

Lifetime deals suit an agency when the tool sits at the edge of your delivery stack: a scraper, a scheduler, a form builder, a transcription tool, an asset library. They suit you badly when the tool is the spine of a client's revenue, because your recovery options if the vendor disappears are thin and capped.

Four things decide the outcome, in order: the license tier you buy on day one, because the upgrade path expires with the deal; whether the deal is code based or license based, because those two scale in opposite directions; what the listing says about seats, workspaces, sub accounts and client use, which is set per deal and not by AppSumo; and the refund window on that specific listing, which is not always 60 days. Browse the current AppSumo catalog with those four in front of you and the shopping trip gets much shorter.

Why sold out is the real deadline

Every agency treats the countdown clock on a deal page as the deadline. It is not. The real deadline is the sell out, and AppSumo says so itself in its licensing support article, last updated May 22, 2026: once a deal has sold out of the marketplace you will only see the option to downgrade, because there are no additional licensing tiers available for purchase. The same article adds that downgrades can only be requested within the number of days specified on the deal page.

Read as an agency, that is blunt: your capacity ceiling is set at checkout. If Tier 1 covers three client workspaces and you buy it to test, you have not bought an option on Tier 3. You have bought three workspaces, possibly forever.

The code based catalog has the same trap phrased more gently. AppSumo's stacking article, last updated May 20, 2026, says you can start with one code, test it, then stack more later if you want additional features, and puts the important part in a parenthesis: before it sells out. Same ceiling, different mechanic, and in both cases the warning lives in a support article rather than on the page where you spend the money. Check what is still in stock before you plan around a tier.

Codes stack, licenses do not

Two different products wearing the same badge, and agencies get caught by the difference constantly.

  • Code based deals stack. You buy multiple codes for the same product to unlock a higher plan or more features. The number of codes you buy equals the number of listings in your account. Stacking is available at each partner's discretion and is stated in the Deal Terms section of the listing, so it is not universal.
  • License based deals do not stack. You change tier instead, up or down, through the Change plan action on the Products page of your account.

One number worth knowing if you buy for a roster of clients: AppSumo applies a quantity limit at checkout, and its own guidance is to buy nine codes in one transaction and any extras in a second. A fifteen code stack means two checkouts.

The agency rule: with code based deals you can scale in steps while the deal is live, so buying one to test is defensible. With license based deals, buying the entry tier to test is a bet that the deal will still be on sale when you need more. That is the bet that loses.

Can an agency use a deal for client work?

This is the question that sends agency owners into forum threads. The distinction that matters is narrower than most people assume.

AppSumo's Terms prohibit reselling the product. Section 5D says you cannot resell any product purchased through the service or use it to trade or barter with others. What the Terms nowhere say is that you cannot use a tool you bought to perform work for a paying client. Using a scraper you own to build a lead list for a client is service delivery. Handing that client a seat, a login, or a code so they own the software is closer to the thing the Terms forbid.

Where the line sits exactly is not set by AppSumo. It is set per deal, by the partner, in the Deal Terms on the listing: how many seats, how many workspaces or sub accounts, whether white labelling is included, whether client billing is allowed. Read that box before the pricing table. If it is silent, AppSumo's own recommended route is the Questions feature on the listing, which puts the answer in public where you can point at it later. Our lead generation team runs this check before adding any tool to a client workflow.

Three documents, three different penalties

No deal roundup mentions this. AppSumo describes the consequence of reselling in three separate places, and the three do not agree.

  • The help centre article on reselling, last updated May 10, 2023, says customers who resell and rebuy outside the site risk having their account permanently deactivated. That is the page a curious agency owner actually lands on.
  • Terms of Use section 5D, last modified February 11, 2025, is harsher and more specific. AppSumo may cancel your purchase and deactivate access to the product, will not refund you, and, in the clause almost nobody quotes, you agree to pay AppSumo the amount of money you made by violating the provision.
  • Terms of Use section 5B then widens the blast radius. It lists reselling in violation of the Terms as one of the things that makes a customer not in good standing, and the remedy there is to limit, suspend, or terminate your account and accounts associated with you.

Put those together and the exposure is not one deal. Section 5D reads as though the penalty is scoped to the product in question. Section 5B, written for a different purpose elsewhere in the document, extends it to the whole account and to associated accounts. For an agency holding a locker of sixty lifetime deals, that is the entire locker. The customer facing help page is also roughly twenty one months older than the binding Terms it links to, and omits the money clause entirely. The Terms govern, not the friendly summary.

What the refund and guarantee cover

Three limits worth having in writing before you spend agency money.

The refund window is per deal. The Terms state that refund periods vary by product and category, that lifetime deals typically carry 60 days from the day of purchase unless otherwise stated, and that some deals offer 30. Check the listing rather than assuming 60.

We Got Your Back is narrower than the name. It returns 100 percent in credits, not cash, only on Select tools, only if the tool closes within one year of purchase, and only for Plus members. A tool you deploy in year one and lose in year three is covered by none of it.

Liability is capped. The Terms limit AppSumo's aggregate liability to the greater of 100 US dollars or what you paid in the past twelve months, and state that claims about a product must be brought directly against the seller, with disputes going to binding arbitration in Austin, Texas under Texas law and a class action waiver. If a tool holding client data fails, AppSumo is not the counterparty. The vendor is.

On data, the Terms treat AppSumo and each partner as independent data controllers. If your agency is a processor for a client, the vendor behind the deal is effectively a sub processor in that chain, and your client contract probably has something to say about naming them.

Where lifetime deals belong in a stack

AppSumo's own help page cites an estimated 92 percent failure rate for SaaS companies in their first three years, and says that of the thousands of tools launched on AppSumo, only around 5 percent have gone under. Both are AppSumo's figures rather than independent audits, so treat them as directional. Even on the friendlier one, roughly one in twenty tools you buy will eventually stop existing. That is fine on a tool that formats images. It is not fine on the system holding your client's pipeline.

  • Good fit: anything you could replace in an afternoon. Scrapers, enrichment top ups, schedulers, form and proposal builders, transcription, design assets, internal dashboards.
  • Bad fit: your CRM, your sending infrastructure, client billing, anything holding data you would migrate under pressure. Those belong on vendors with a support contract, which is why we keep our GoHighLevel work off the deal market.
  • Export test: before a tool touches client data, confirm you can get the data out in a standard format, inside the refund window.

The five checks to run before you buy

About four minutes per deal, and the whole difference between a stack that scales and a drawer of dead codes.

  • 1. Read the Deal Terms box before the pricing table. Seats, workspaces, sub accounts, client use, white labelling, stackability. If client work is not addressed, ask on the listing.
  • 2. Buy the tier that matches next year's client count. The upgrade path dies when the deal sells out.
  • 3. Check whether it is code based or license based. Codes stack while the deal is live. Licenses change tier and cannot stack.
  • 4. Confirm the refund window on that listing. Sixty days is the default, not a guarantee, and 30 day deals exist.
  • 5. Redeem and test inside the window. AppSumo's own advice is that the refund period is the only time your purchase is fully protected. An unredeemed code past day 60 is a donation.

On the membership: AppSumo Plus costs 99 dollars a year for 10 percent off every deal, 100 dollars in coupons issued as 25 dollars every 90 days, free KingSumo and SendFox at License Tier 1, faster support, and the credit guarantee above. The catch that belongs in an honest guide is that Plus is explicitly non refundable. At around 1,000 dollars of annual spend it pays for itself on the discount and coupons alone. Below that it does not, and you cannot undo it.

If the bottleneck is pipeline rather than tooling, no lifetime deal fixes that. Check the current AppSumo deals for the edges of your stack, and keep the core on software you can call someone about.
faqs: Can my agency use an AppSumo lifetime deal for client work?

AppSumo's Terms of Use prohibit reselling a product or trading and bartering it, but they do not prohibit using a tool you own to deliver services to a paying client. What decides how many client seats, workspaces or sub accounts you get is the per deal license tier and the partner's own Deal Terms on the listing, not AppSumo policy. Read that box before you buy, and if it is silent on client use, ask on the listing's Questions feature so the answer is public.
Can I upgrade my license tier later once I have more clients?

Only while the deal is still on sale. AppSumo's licensing support article states that once a deal has sold out of the marketplace you will only see the option to downgrade, because there are no additional licensing tiers available for purchase. Downgrades are also limited to the number of days specified on the deal page. For code based deals the same limit applies in a different form: you can stack more codes later, but only before the deal sells out.
What happens if I give a client access to a deal I bought?

It depends whether you are sharing seats the license grants you or effectively transferring the product. Terms section 5D says AppSumo may cancel the purchase, deactivate access, refuse a refund, and that you agree to pay AppSumo the amount of money you made by violating the clause. Section 5B separately treats reselling as putting you out of good standing, which allows AppSumo to limit, suspend or terminate your account and accounts associated with you. Accounts are also not transferable under section 3.
Is AppSumo Plus worth it for an agency?

AppSumo Plus costs 99 dollars a year and includes 10 percent off every deal, 100 dollars in coupons issued as 25 dollars every 90 days, free KingSumo and SendFox at License Tier 1, faster support and the We Got Your Back credit guarantee. It breaks even for most agencies at roughly 1,000 dollars of annual AppSumo spend. The important caveat is that Plus is explicitly non refundable, so below that spend level it is a loss you cannot reverse.
What is the refund window on an AppSumo lifetime deal?

It is set per deal. AppSumo's Terms state that refund periods vary by product and category, that lifetime deals typically carry a 60 day window beginning the day of purchase unless otherwise stated, and that some deals offer 30 days instead. Digital books cannot be returned at all. Check the specific listing rather than assuming 60 days, and redeem and test the tool inside the window, which AppSumo itself describes as the only time your purchase is fully protected.
What happens to my agency if a lifetime deal tool shuts down?

Usually very little recourse, which is why lifetime deals belong at the edge of a delivery stack rather than the core. AppSumo's We Got Your Back guarantee returns 100 percent in credits rather than cash, and only for Select tools that close within one year of purchase, and only for Plus members. The Terms cap AppSumo's aggregate liability at the greater of 100 US dollars or what you paid in the past twelve months and direct product claims to the seller.
